lesson.text: Data remembers why it was given.

Purpose limitation is the principle that personal data collected for one reason may not simply be reused for another. Data must be gathered for purposes that are SPECIFIED, EXPLICIT, and LEGITIMATE — and not further used in ways INCOMPATIBLE with those. You spent an afternoon at Quill's desk applying exactly this: matching each request against the ledger's original purpose.

THE PURPOSE MUST BE FIXED FIRST — You cannot judge a reuse without a clearly recorded ORIGINAL purpose. 'We collected it, so we may use it' is the error the principle exists to kill. The ledger — the record of why data was given — is the reference point for every later decision.

But purpose limitation is not a wall that forbids all reuse. The real question is COMPATIBILITY: is the new purpose closely enough related to the original that a reasonable person who gave the data would not be surprised? The law names factors to weigh this: the LINK between old and new purpose, the CONTEXT in which data was collected, the NATURE of the data (sensitive data raises the bar), the CONSEQUENCES for the person, and whether SAFEGUARDS (like anonymization) are applied.

THREE OUTCOMES (the desk you worked):
COMPATIBLE → the reuse may proceed. (Announcing music is scheduling.)
INCOMPATIBLE → it may NOT proceed on the old basis; it needs a fresh lawful basis or new consent. (Billing records repurposed for marketing.)
COMPATIBLE WITH SAFEGUARDS → permissible only once conditioned: anonymize/aggregate so no individual is exposed, or seek fresh consent. (Health visit counts for planning a well — but by district, never by name.)

Two errors sit on either side, and a good archivist avoids both. SCOPE CREEP is reusing data for a convenient, incompatible new purpose (the Merchants' trick). But OVER-RESTRICTION is refusing a genuinely compatible use out of mere suspicion — that blocks legitimate work and, ironically, tempts people to collect fresh data they didn't need. Read the purpose, not your reflex.

GOOD INTENTIONS ARE NOT THE TEST — The Tinkers meant well — better roads, a new well. Worthy aims do not make an incompatible purpose compatible. Compatibility is judged on the factors above, not on the virtue of the requester. A noble reuse of the wrong data still needs to ask afresh.

Purpose limitation is also why you MINIMISE and why you set RETENTION limits: if data may serve only its purpose, then once the purpose is served, the data has no reason to remain. Specify the purpose, honour it, and let everything else — extra fields, extra time, extra uses — fall away.

cases.scenario: Before he'll let you touch the ledger unsupervised, Quill poses one question: a request lands on the desk to reuse data for something new. What must be true before you can even begin judging it?
verdicts: The requester is trustworthy
The ORIGINAL specified purpose is on record
The data is encrypted
consequence: You wave through a request from someone respectable, no ledger check made — and a week later a perfectly untrustworthy requester's IDENTICAL request sails through too, because "trustworthy" was never a real test to begin with.
You pull the original ledger entry first, every time — and Quill nods. Whatever the verdict turns out to be, at least it will be judged against something real.
You check whether the data is encrypted, hand it over, and only later realize encryption never once asked whether the NEW use was any of the requester's business.
explain: Trustworthiness isn't the test — even a trusted requester can't licence an incompatible reuse, and an untrusted one can still ask for something genuinely compatible.
Correct — compatibility is measured against why the data was collected. No recorded purpose, no way to judge reuse — the ledger comes first.
Encryption protects data in transit or storage; it says nothing about whether a NEW use of it is compatible with why it was collected.

cases.scenario: Tavern tab records, collected to settle billing disputes, are requested by a merchant to market hangover potions to heavy drinkers.
verdicts: GRANT
CONDITIONAL
SEAL
consequence: The merchant builds a full drinking-habits profile from records that were only ever meant to settle bar tabs — every regular at the Griffin's Drink now has a marketing target painted on their back.
You reach for a safeguard, but there isn't one that fixes this — the tab data itself IS the marketing profile. Conditioning it just delays the same harm.
You seal the request and tell the merchant plainly: come back with the tavern's actual patrons' consent, or don't come back at all. Billing stays billing.
explain: Granting this lets billing data become a marketing profile — exactly the harm purpose limitation exists to stop.
No safeguard fixes this — the problem isn't exposure risk, it's that marketing was never the purpose at all.
Correct — billing to marketing is a classic incompatible repurposing (scope creep). It needs a fresh lawful basis / consent, not the billing purpose stretched to cover it.
cases.hint: Ask only one thing: was this NEW use foreseeable within the reason the data was first collected — not whether it's profitable, harmless-sounding, or well-intentioned.

variant.scenario: Guardhouse shift logs, kept to track who's on duty, are requested by a merchant to time deliveries around guard rotations.
verdicts: GRANT
CONDITIONAL
SEAL
consequence: The merchant now knows exactly when the watch changes at every gate — a shift log meant to track duty rosters just became a map of the village's weakest hours.
No safeguard turns a rotation schedule into something safe to hand a merchant — the problem is the PURPOSE, not the exposure.
You seal it. If deliveries need scheduling, the merchant can ask the guard captain directly — not read it off a duty roster never meant to leave the guardhouse.
explain: Granting hands a merchant a live map of security gaps — a shift log becoming a delivery-timing tool is scope creep with real risk.
No safeguard converts this — the problem isn't exposure, it's that commercial delivery-timing was never the purpose of a shift log.
Correct — shift-tracking to commercial delivery-timing is incompatible repurposing. It needs its own lawful basis, not the shift log's purpose stretched to cover it.

cases.scenario: A guild wants health-visit data to decide where to dig a new well — a genuinely useful, compatible aim. The data names patients.
verdicts: GRANT the raw data — the purpose is compatible
CONDITIONAL: aggregate to district counts first
SEAL — health data can never be reused
consequence: The guild gets a list of exactly who has been treated for what, and where they live — a genuinely good idea for the village now doubles as a directory of everyone's health history.
The guild gets district-level counts — enough to see where the need is greatest, nothing that points back to a single named patient. The well gets dug; no one's history leaves the desk.

You refuse outright, and the guild digs the well somewhere convenient instead of somewhere needed — the good the compatible purpose could have done never happens, for no real gain in anyone's protection.
explain: The purpose being compatible doesn't clear raw, named health data — sensitive data raises the bar, and a safeguard is owed before it travels.
Correct — the purpose is compatible, but sensitive data raises the bar: condition it by anonymizing to counts so the good deed exposes no one. Neither blanket grant nor blanket refusal.
Health data isn't sealed forever — a compatible purpose plus the right safeguard lets it serve a new, worthy aim without exposing anyone.

cases.scenario: A request SOUNDS invasive — "list who attended each performance" — but the ledger shows attendance was gathered to program the festival, and the use is to choose which acts to rebook.
verdicts: SEAL — it sounds like surveillance
GRANT — it matches the original programming purpose
CONDITIONAL — always condition attendance data
consequence: You seal a request that was never a threat — next year's festival gets programmed blind, worse for everyone, and the only thing you protected was your own discomfort with how the request SOUNDED.
The programmer gets exactly what they need to decide which acts return — the same purpose the attendance was recorded for in the first place. Nothing new was exposed.
You bolt a safeguard onto a request that never needed one — the programmer waits on an aggregation step that protects no one, because this was never a risky use to begin with.
explain: Sealing a compatible use out of reflex is OVER-RESTRICTION — the mirror error of scope creep. It blocks legitimate work for no real gain in protection.
Correct — compatibility is judged on the purpose, not on how sinister it feels. Attendance recorded to shape the programme, used to shape the programme — that's the same purpose.
Conditioning every request "just in case" isn't free — it delays or degrades legitimate work that never needed a safeguard in the first place.

cases.scenario: The Tinkers — decent, well-meaning folk — want the emergency headcounts gathered during the spring evacuation drill, to help plan where a new road should go. It's a good cause.
verdicts: GRANT — their cause is good, and good intentions matter
SEAL on this basis — ask the Tinkers to gather fresh planning data with its own basis
GRANT — but only because the Tinkers are well-known and trusted
consequence: The Tinkers get their road built faster — and every future "good cause" now has precedent to reach into data gathered for something else entirely, because good intentions were treated as a lawful basis.

The Tinkers are turned away from THIS ledger entry, but nothing stops them asking the village council directly for planning data gathered on its own terms — the road still gets built, just not on borrowed data.
You wave it through because you like the Tinkers — and the next requester you don't happen to trust gets held to a standard the Tinkers never had to meet.
explain: Trust and good intentions don't convert an incompatible purpose — emergency crowd-control and road planning are different purposes regardless of how worthy the second one is.
Correct — compatibility is judged on the link, context, and consequences between the two purposes, not on the requester's virtue. The Tinkers need their own basis for road-planning data.
Priority or personal trust has nothing to do with it — even a well-known, likable requester still needs a compatible purpose or a fresh basis.

cases.scenario: A tailor collects a customer's measurements to complete a commissioned coat, and separately asks if she may email her about a new autumn line.
verdicts: The COMMISSION (contract) covers both — a coat needs measurements, and telling her about new items is good service
The COMMISSION covers the coat; the EMAIL needs her separate CONSENT
Neither needs a basis — the tailor already has her details
consequence: The customer starts getting seasonal marketing emails she never agreed to, because "good service" quietly became the tailor's excuse to skip asking.
The coat gets made under the commission, and the customer gets asked — plainly — whether she wants autumn-line emails. She says yes or no, and either way, it was actually her choice.
The tailor emails her anyway, on the theory that having her address once means having it forever, for anything — exactly the assumption purpose limitation exists to forbid.
explain: The commission covers taking and using measurements to make the coat — it doesn't stretch to cover a marketing email about something else entirely.
Correct — fulfilling the coat is necessary for the CONTRACT; emailing about new items is a separate purpose that needs its own basis, here her freely given CONSENT.
Both bases exist for a reason — collecting and using data always needs one; there's no license to skip asking.
cases.hint: Ask which action was actually NECESSARY to deliver on the contract, and which one was optional, additional, and needed the customer's own yes.

variant.scenario: A healer takes a patient's address to deliver medicine ordered under treatment, and separately asks to add her to a mailing list for seasonal remedies.
verdicts: The TREATMENT (contract) covers both — delivery needs an address, and the mailing list is a courtesy
The TREATMENT covers delivery; the MAILING LIST needs her separate CONSENT
Neither — healers don't need a basis
consequence: The patient starts getting seasonal remedy flyers she never asked for, because delivering her medicine was quietly stretched to cover marketing too.
The medicine gets delivered under the treatment, and the healer asks separately whether she'd like seasonal remedy notices — freely given, and just as freely revocable.
The healer signs her up without asking, on the theory that treating her once means her address is fair game for anything after — exactly the assumption purpose limitation forbids.
explain: The treatment contract covers delivering the ordered medicine — it doesn't extend to unrelated seasonal marketing.
Correct — delivering medicine is necessary for the CONTRACT; the mailing list is a separate purpose resting on her own CONSENT, freely given and revocable.
Healers handle personal data like anyone else — every use still needs its own lawful basis.
